topic: What Dürer hid in a magic square

opening.say: In fifteen fourteen, an artist named Albrecht Dürer put a small grid of numbers into one of his engravings.
It's called a magic square, and the magic is that every row adds up to the very same total.
But Dürer wasn't content with rows alone. He tucked far more sums into that grid, and one is a secret.

more.say: Try a tiny case first. In a three by three square, every row, every column, and both long diagonals add to fifteen.
So the rule isn't just rows. A magic square keeps one total across many different lines, and that's what makes it feel designed.
Dürer's grid is bigger, so it has more places to hide matching totals. Let's go hunting through his square.

plan.setup: Watch which cells light up together.
plan.narration: [[grid-appears]]Here's his grid, using the numbers one through sixteen. [[rows-light]]Every row adds to thirty-four. [[cols-diags]]So does every column, and both diagonals. [[corners-quad]]Now the surprise: the four corners also make thirty-four. [[center-quad]]So do the four middle cells. [[date-row]]And in the bottom row, the middle pair reads fifteen fourteen.
plan.plan:
grid-appears: a four by four grid shows Dürer's square, rows sixteen three two thirteen; five ten eleven eight; nine six seven twelve; four fifteen fourteen one.
rows-light: each row highlights in turn, labelled sum equals thirty-four.
cols-diags: columns then both diagonals highlight, each again labelled thirty-four.
corners-quad: the four corner cells sixteen, thirteen, four, one glow together, totalling thirty-four.
center-quad: the central four cells ten, eleven, six, seven glow, also thirty-four.
date-row: bottom row's middle cells fifteen and fourteen circle, showing the year.
plan.close: Can you find another group of four cells that adds to thirty-four?
